hints: Write the equation $2\text{HBr}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_{2}(\text{g}) + \text{Br}_{2}(\text{g})$ and count how many moles of each bond are broken and formed.
walkthrough:
Separate breaking from making**
Think of bond energies as the cost to break bonds. Breaking needs energy in, so positive. Making releases energy out. The rule you always use is $$\Delta H = \text{(energy to break bonds)} - \text{(energy released making bonds)}$$ For $2\text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2} + \text{Br}_{2}$ you break $2$ moles of $\text{H-Br}$ and you make $1$ mole of $\text{H-H}$ plus $1$ mole of $\text{Br-Br}$.

Put the numbers in**
Breaking: $2 \times 366 = 732 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Making: $436 + 193 = 629 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. So $$\Delta H = 732 - 629 = +103 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Positive fits an endothermic decomposition.
Final answer: $\Delta H = +103 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Recall what higher temperature does to the average molecular energy and to the spread of energies, while total number of molecules stays the same.
Think about the three sketch rules: start point, peak height and position, and where the new curve must finish relative to the original.
walkthrough:
Picture what heating does**
At higher T molecules on average move faster, so the whole spread of energies shifts to higher values. No molecules have zero energy, so you must still start at the origin. Because total area under the curve is total number of molecules, which has not changed, if the curve spreads out it must get lower at the peak.

Draw the new curve correctly**
Keep the same axes. Start at $(0,0)$. Draw a flatter, wider hump with its maximum to the right of the original maximum and clearly lower. Let it cross the original curve once on the right hand side, then stay above the original all the way along the high energy tail, because more molecules now have very high energy.

Final answer: Curve starts at origin, with broader shape, peak lower than original and displaced to the right (higher energy). Curve crosses original once only and finishes above original at high energy.

hints: Look at the area under each Boltzmann curve to the right of $E_a$ and compare the 700 K curve with the higher T curve.
Recall the two conditions for a successful collision: correct orientation and energy greater than or equal to $E_a$.
Link more frequent successful collisions to rate, remembering that collision frequency also increases slightly but the dominant effect is the $E \geqslant E_a$ factor.
walkthrough:
Read the area beyond Ea**
Only molecules with energy at or beyond $E_a$ can react when they collide. On your sketch the area under the high T curve to the right of $E_a$ is clearly larger than for the 700 K curve. That area is the number of molecules able to react.

Explain why rate goes up**
Heating gives many more molecules enough energy to overcome the barrier. Molecules also move faster so they collide more often, but the big effect is that a much larger proportion of those collisions are now successful.

State the rate conclusion**
More successful collisions per unit time means faster breaking of $\text{H-Br}$ bonds, so the rate of decomposition of $\text{HBr}$ increases. Keep rate and extent separate here, this part is only about how fast.

Final answer: Rate of decomposition increases.
At higher T a greater area is above $E_a$ / more molecules have $E \geqslant E_a$.
There is a higher frequency of successful collisions per unit time / greater proportion of successful collisions.

hints: Identify which direction in $2\text{HBr} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_{2} + \text{Br}_{2}$ is endothermic from part (a).
Recall Le Chatelier's idea: the equilibrium shifts to oppose an imposed temperature rise by absorbing heat.
Translate a rightward shift into what happens to the amount of $\text{HBr}$ remaining versus products formed.
walkthrough:
Spot the heat direction**
From (a) $\Delta H = +103 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for $2\text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2} + \text{Br}_{2}$. Forward is endothermic, it takes in heat. Backward is exothermic, it gives out heat.

Apply Le Chatelier**
Le Chatelier says if you raise temperature, the system tries to cool itself down by favouring the reaction that absorbs heat. So equilibrium moves to the right, in the endothermic direction.

Link to percentage**
Moving right uses up more $\text{HBr}$ and makes more $\text{H}_{2}$ and $\text{Br}_{2}$. Therefore a larger percentage of the original $\text{HBr}$ is decomposed at equilibrium.

Final answer: Percentage decomposition of $\text{HBr}$ increases.
Increasing T shifts equilibrium to the right / forward / endothermic direction towards $\text{H}_{2} + \text{Br}_{2}$.
This opposes the temperature rise by absorbing heat / lowering temperature.

hints: Compare the extent of decomposition: $\text{HI}$ decomposes more, so decide whether $\text{H-I}$ is stronger or weaker than $\text{H-Br}$.
Compare the sizes of $\text{Br}$ and $\text{I}$ atoms and think about distance of bonding electrons from the nucleus and shielding.
Think about how well a small $1\text{s}$ orbital on H can overlap with a large diffuse $5\text{p}$ orbital on I versus a smaller $4\text{p}$ orbital on Br.
walkthrough:
Translate percentage into bond strength**
More decomposition means the bond breaks more easily. If $20$% of $\text{HI}$ breaks but only $10$% of $\text{HBr}$ breaks at the same T, the $\text{H-I}$ bond must be weaker and need less energy to break.

Explain with atomic size**
Iodine is below bromine in Group 17. Its outer electrons are in the $n=5$ shell, further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells than bromine ($n=4$). So the bonding pair is further out and less strongly attracted to the iodine nucleus.

Add the overlap idea**
The $\text{H-I}$ bond forms by overlap of H $1\text{s}$ with a large, diffuse I $5\text{p}$ orbital. Overlap is less effective than with the smaller Br $4\text{p}$ orbital, so the bond is longer and weaker. Weaker bonds break faster and give a larger equilibrium decomposition.

Final answer: $\text{H-I}$ bond is weaker than $\text{H-Br}$ / less energy needed to break $\text{H-I}$.
Iodine atom is larger than bromine / has more shielding.
Poorer orbital overlap in $\text{H-I}$ / weaker nuclear attraction for the shared pair in $\text{H-I}$.

hints: Use the equation $2\text{HCl} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_{2} + \text{Cl}_{2}$ to relate moles of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ formed to moles of $\text{H}_{2}$ formed.
Relate moles of $\text{HCl}$ decomposed to moles of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ formed using the 2:1 ratio, then subtract from the initial 0.300 mol.
walkthrough:
Find moles of H2**
The equation is $$2\text{HCl}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_{2}(\text{g}) + \text{Cl}_{2}(\text{g})$$ One mole of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ is made with one mole of $\text{H}_{2}$. So $$n(\text{H}_{2}) = n(\text{Cl}_{2}) = 1.50 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol} = 0.015 \text{ mol}$$

Find moles of HCl left**
Two moles of $\text{HCl}$ decompose for each mole of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ formed. Moles $\text{HCl}$ reacted $= 2 \times 1.50 \times 10^{-2} = 3.00 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$. Moles left $$= 0.300 - 0.0300 = 0.270 \text{ mol}$$

Final answer: $\text{H}_{2} = 0.015 \text{ mol}$ ($1.50 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$)
$\text{HCl} = 0.27 \text{ mol}$

hints: First add all equilibrium moles to get total moles, then divide each individual amount by this total.
walkthrough:
Divide by the total**
Total moles $= 0.27 + 0.015 + 0.015 = 0.30 \text{ mol}$. Mole fraction $= \frac{\text{moles of gas}}{\text{total moles}}$. So $$x_{\text{HCl}} = \frac{0.27}{0.30} = 0.90$$ $$x_{\text{H}_{2}} = \frac{0.015}{0.30} = 0.05$$ $$x_{\text{Cl}_{2}} = \frac{0.015}{0.30} = 0.05$$ They sum to $1.00$, a good check.
Final answer: mole fraction $\text{HCl} = 0.90$, mole fraction $\text{H}_{2} = 0.05$, mole fraction $\text{Cl}_{2} = 0.05$

hints: Recall $K_p$ uses partial pressures with products on top, reactants below, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient.
walkthrough:
Build the Kp expression**
For $$2\text{HCl}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_{2}(\text{g}) + \text{Cl}_{2}(\text{g})$$ put product partial pressures on top and reactant partial pressures below. The $2$ in front of $\text{HCl}$ becomes a square. So $$K_{p} = \frac{p_{\text{H}_{2}} \times p_{\text{Cl}_{2}}}{p_{\text{HCl}}^{2}}$$ No units are needed for this step, just the correct expression.

hints: Write each partial pressure as mole fraction $\times$ total pressure $P$ and count how many $P$ terms appear on top versus below.
walkthrough:
See why P cancels**
Partial pressure $= $ mole fraction $\times P$. So $$K_{p} = \frac{(x_{\text{H}_{2}}P)(x_{\text{Cl}_{2}}P)}{(x_{\text{HCl}}P)^{2}} = \frac{x_{\text{H}_{2}}x_{\text{Cl}_{2}}P^{2}}{x_{\text{HCl}}^{2}P^{2}}$$ There are $2$ moles of gas on the left and $1+1=2$ on the right, so $P^{2}$ top and bottom cancel. $K_{p}$ can be found from mole fractions alone.
Final answer: Equal number of moles of gas on each side of equation so total pressure cancels.

hints: Substitute the given mole fractions 0.88, 0.06 and 0.06 directly into the $K_p$ expression from (d)(i).
walkthrough:
Substitute and calculate**
Using mole fractions in place of partial pressures because $P$ cancels: $$K_{p} = \frac{0.06 \times 0.06}{0.88^{2}}$$ $$K_{p} = \frac{0.0036}{0.7744} = 4.649 \times 10^{-3}$$ No units, as $P$ has cancelled.
Final answer: $K_{p} = 4.649 \times 10^{-3}$
